title: Carbon–carbon bond formation and organic synthesis; SN1 vs SN2
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR26b#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR10#t2 term and clue written for the game; OR10#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR26b#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR10#N.4, OR26b#N.4, OR10#N.6, OR26b#N.11, OR10#N.10, OR26b#N.16, OR10#N.13, OR10#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Reduction
items.clue: Type of step that turns an aldehyde or ketone into an alcohol.

items.label: SN1
items.clue: Two-step substitution typical of tertiary halogenoalkanes, with rate = k[RBr].

items.label: Transition state
items.clue: Energy maximum with partial bonds, found at the top of a hump on an energy profile.

items.label: Nitrile
items.clue: Functional group made using KCN in ethanol under reflux, adding one carbon to the chain.

questions.stem: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN1 mechanism. Which describes the first step?

options.text: The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻.
OH⁻ attacks the C atom as the C–Br bond breaks, in a single step.
The C–Br bond breaks homolytically, giving radicals (CH₃)₃C• and Br•.
The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁻ and Br⁺ ions.

questions.explanation: The slow first step: Br takes the bonding pair (arrow from the C–Br bond to Br), giving a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻. OH⁻ attacks in the fast second step.

questions.stem: Which compound reacts with KCN in ethanol to give butanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH₂CN?

options.text: 1-Bromobutane
1-Bromopropane
2-Bromopropane
Propanal

questions.explanation: CN⁻ replaces Br on the end carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br → CH₃CH₂CH₂CN. 3 + 1 = 4 carbons.

questions.stem: A halogenoalkane, RX, is hydrolysed by OH⁻(aq). Illustrative initial-rate data: - Exp 1: [RX] 0.010, [OH⁻] 0.10 mol dm⁻³ → rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ - Exp 2: [RX] 0.020, [OH⁻] 0.10 mol dm⁻³ → rate 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ - Exp 3: [RX] 0.010, [OH⁻] 0.20 mol dm⁻³ → rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ Which rate equation and mechanism fit?

options.text: rate = k[RX][OH⁻]; SN2, with both species in one step
rate = k[OH⁻]; SN2, as OH⁻ is the attacking species
rate = k[RX]; SN2, because this mechanism has two steps
rate = k[RX]; SN1, with RX alone in the slow step

questions.explanation: First order in RX (Exp 1→2), zero order in OH⁻ (Exp 1→3). Only RX is in the rate-determining step: C–X breaks to a carbocation. Likely tertiary.

options.text: Mg in dry ether, then propanal, then dilute acid
Mg in dry ether, then propanone, then dilute acid
Mg in dry ether, then CO₂, then dilute acid
KCN in ethanol, then propanone, then hydrolyse with acid

questions.explanation: CH₃CH₂MgBr adds to the C=O of propanone: a tertiary alcohol with five carbons, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃.

questions.stem: A single enantiomer of 3-bromo-3-methylhexane rotates plane-polarised light. After hydrolysis with OH⁻(aq), the 3-methylhexan-3-ol formed does not rotate the light. What does this show?

options.text: SN2: OH⁻ attacked from the back, so the configuration was inverted.
SN1: the planar carbocation was attacked from both faces equally.
SN2: the transition state is planar, so a racemic mixture forms.
SN1: the alcohol has no chiral centre, so it can't rotate the light.

questions.explanation: Equal attack on each face gives a racemic mixture. The two enantiomers' rotations cancel, so there is no net rotation.

questions.stem: A chemist needs 2-hydroxybutanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN, and has propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Which two-step plan works?

options.text: Oxidise with acidified dichromate(VI) under reflux; then add cyanide to it
Dehydrate with a hot acid catalyst to give propene; then add cyanide
Add cyanide to the alcohol first; then oxidise with acidified dichromate(VI)
Oxidise with acidified dichromate(VI) and distil; then add cyanide

questions.explanation: Working back: a hydroxynitrile comes from an aldehyde + cyanide; propanal comes from propan-1-ol, distilled out as it forms.

questions.stem: Which statement about the mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes is correct?

options.text: Secondary ones react by SN1 and SN2, as both paths are feasible.
Primary ones react by SN1, as their carbocations are most stable.
Tertiary ones react by SN1, which takes place in one step.
Primary ones react via a stable intermediate with five bonds to C.

questions.explanation: Primary react by SN2 and tertiary by SN1. A secondary carbocation is of intermediate stability and backside attack only partly hindered, so both occur.

questions.stem: Two isomers of C₅H₁₁Cl are each hydrolysed by OH⁻(aq). Doubling [OH⁻] doubles the rate for 1-chloropentane, but leaves the rate unchanged for 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Which statement is correct?

options.text: 1-chloropentane: SN1 via a carbocation · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN2 in one step
1-chloropentane: SN2 in two steps · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN1 in one step
1-chloropentane: SN2 in one step · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN1 via a carbocation
1-chloropentane: SN2 via an intermediate · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN1 via a carbocation

questions.explanation: Primary: OH⁻ in the one step, rate = k[RCl][OH⁻]. Tertiary: slow C–Cl break to a stable tertiary carbocation, rate = k[RCl].
